patient.name: Joan Whitfield
patient.setting: Elderly care ward, Whipps Cross Hospital (day 6 of admission)
patient.complaint: New watery, foul-smelling diarrhoea, seven times since last night, with cramping abdominal pain
background: Admitted with community-acquired pneumonia: IV co-amoxiclav, then ceftriaxone
Omeprazole 20 mg for reflux for years
Codeine for a painful hip; type 2 diabetes

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely causative organism?' with new watery diarrhoea after broad-spectrum antibiotics or PPIs (C. difficile), bloody diarrhoea and fever after chicken (Campylobacter) or after travel (Entamoeba), and questions on antigen versus toxin results and severity (WCC >15, creatinine rise >50%).

points: Day 6 in hospital for pneumonia; chest improving.
Overnight: **seven watery, green, foul-smelling stools** with mucus.
Crampy pain all over her abdomen; nauseated.
Dry mouth; she is passing less urine.

steps.lead: Joan's new diarrhoea is likely **infective colitis**: bacteria, viruses or parasites inflaming the colon.

steps.r: New watery diarrhoea in hospital after **broad-spectrum antibiotics** and a **PPI**: C. difficile until proven otherwise.

steps.lead: Joan has the classic risk set: **co-amoxiclav and ceftriaxone**, long-term **omeprazole**, older age, in hospital. C. difficile is an **anaerobic Gram-positive** bacterium.
Joan's stool is the C. difficile pattern: **watery, green, foul-smelling, mucus-mixed**, with cramps, a diffusely tender abdomen and dehydration.

visual.title: Where Joan is tender
visual.caption: Diffuse tenderness fits colitis. Rising distension and silence would suggest toxic megacolon.

steps.title: Which colitis is it?
head: Organism
Stool
Clue
rows: Food, contacts; E. coli O157 → HUS

steps.lead: When Joan's stool comes back, a positive **antigen** alone would mean only colonisation; a positive **toxin** means true infection.
Joan will be classed as **severe** if her WCC is over 15 or her creatinine rises more than 50%; **toxic megacolon** makes it life-threatening.

steps.text: Stop Joan's **codeine** and never give loperamide: slowing the gut in C. difficile predisposes to **toxic megacolon**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which result confirms active infection?' (toxin, not antigen), 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' (stool culture and toxin testing; CT if severe), and severity from the WCC and creatinine.

steps.q: Which result shows Joan has active C. difficile infection?
steps.r: The **toxin** test confirms infection. Antigen alone shows the bug is there, not that it is causing disease.

steps.lead: Joan's stool goes for **C. difficile toxin testing** plus culture and PCR: toxin is what separates infection from carriage.

steps.title: Joan's stool results
rows: Stool culture (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, E. coli O157)
steps.text: Antigen plus toxin: true C. difficile infection.

steps.lead: Joan's bloods: **FBC** for the white cell count, **CRP**, and **U&Es** for dehydration and kidney injury.

visual.title: White cell count: C. difficile severity
visual.label: Joan 17.6
visual.caption: WCC over 15 alone makes this **severe** C. difficile infection.

visual.title: Joan's creatinine
visual.caption: 118 is a 64% rise from 72: the second severity marker (>50%).

steps.lead: Joan's WCC marks **severe** disease. Her abdomen is soft and not distended, so no **CT** yet; it is done if severe complications are suspected.

steps.title: Grading C. difficile severity
nodes: Mild/moderate: WCC normal or raised up to 15
Life-threatening: shock, ileus, toxic megacolon, severe dilatation on CT
steps.caption: The grade decides whether to add IV metronidazole and call the surgeons.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (oral vancomycin for 10 days and stop the culprit antibiotic), the second-line (fidaxomicin, e.g. recurrence within 12 weeks), the life-threatening combination (oral vancomycin plus IV metronidazole) and infection control (soap and water).

points: Joan's pneumonia antibiotics are reviewed and stopped.
She is moved to a **side room** with an en-suite.

steps.r: **Oral** vancomycin (it must reach the colon lumen). IV vancomycin is not excreted into the gut.

steps.lead: Joan stops the causative antibiotic and starts **oral vancomycin for 10 days**; she stays isolated until **48 hours** free of diarrhoea.
Staff use **gloves, aprons** and **soap and water**; Joan gets oral rehydration, with **IV 0.9% saline** while she cannot keep up.

steps.text: **Alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores.** Only soap and water hand washing works.

steps.lead: If Joan fails to respond, or relapses within **12 weeks**, she gets **oral fidaxomicin**; if still no response, vancomycin ± IV metronidazole.
Had Joan become shocked or developed megacolon, she would need **oral vancomycin plus IV metronidazole** and urgent surgical review.

head: Situation
Treatment
rows: No response or recurrence within 12 weeks

visual.title: Joan's response to oral vancomycin
visual.caption: Fewer stools and a falling WCC mean response; no improvement by day 5 or so should prompt a review.

steps.lead: Joan's plan follows **NICE/UKHSA C. difficile guidance** and **antimicrobial stewardship** principles: right drug, review, stop.

steps.text: Treat Joan's colitis, but also **prevent the next one**: stewardship of antibiotics and PPIs is what stops C. difficile.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why antibiotics cause C. difficile (loss of colonic flora), how toxins A and B form pseudomembranes, why toxic megacolon occurs, and why alcohol gel fails (spores).

steps.lead: Joan's co-amoxiclav and ceftriaxone wiped out her normal **colonic flora**, letting C. difficile **spores germinate** and multiply.

steps.title: From antibiotic to colitis
steps.caption: Stewardship breaks the chain at the first step.

steps.lead: Joan's diarrhoea is caused by **toxins A and B**; at endoscopy her colon would show raised yellow **pseudomembranes**.
If inflammation becomes **transmural**, Joan's colon loses motility and dilates: **toxic megacolon**, with perforation and sepsis risk.
C. difficile forms **spores**; alcohol gel does not kill them, so soap and water washing **physically removes** them.

steps.q: Why does Joan's omeprazole raise her risk?
o: Less gastric acid lets organisms survive
steps.r: Acid suppression allows more ingested **spores** and bacteria to reach the colon.

steps.text: Antigen = the organism is there. **Toxin = disease.** Spores = why gel fails and why it spreads on wards.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: bloody or not, hospital or travel.

Bacteria: C. difficile, Campylobacter, Shigella, Salmonella, E. coli

Campylobacter, Shigella, Salmonella, E. coli: bloody diarrhoea and fever

prompts.q: How do you interpret C. difficile antigen and toxin results?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: antigen alone is not disease.

prompts.q: What makes C. difficile severe or life-threatening?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two numbers, then four danger signs.

points.p: Life-threatening: sepsis, ileus, dilatation on CT

points.p: Stool culture and toxin testing (gold standard)
CT abdomen if severe disease suspected

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: oral vancomycin, stop, isolate.

points.why: Oral, so it reaches the colon.

points.p: Stop the causative antibiotic (and PPI if possible)
Isolate until 48 hours free of diarrhoea
Rehydrate: ORS first, IV 0.9% saline if needed

prompts.q: What do you do if treatment fails, it recurs, or it is life-threatening?

points.p: Failure or recurrence within 12 weeks: oral fidaxomicin
Still no response: vancomycin with or without IV metronidazole
Life-threatening: oral vancomycin AND IV metronidazole

prompts.q: How do you control infection and manage other bacterial colitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: soap and water; Campylobacter rarely needs antibiotics.

points.p: Soap and water hand washing, not alcohol gel

prompts.q: How does C. difficile cause colitis and toxic megacolon?

points.why: Spores survive on surfaces for months.

points.p: Toxins A and B damage colonic mucosa
Transmural inflammation impairs motility: megacolon, perforation

prompts.q: Why is alcohol gel not enough for C. difficile?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: spores are the answer.

Soap and water physically removes them

glossary.infectious colitis: Inflammation of the colon caused by bacteria, viruses or parasites.
glossary.C. difficile: Clostridioides difficile: spore-forming anaerobic Gram-positive bacterium causing antibiotic-associated colitis.
glossary.Clostridioides difficile: Spore-forming anaerobic Gram-positive bacillus that causes antibiotic-associated colitis.
glossary.pseudomembranous colitis: Severe C. difficile colitis with yellow plaques of fibrin and debris on the colonic lining.
glossary.pseudomembranes: Raised yellow plaques of fibrin, mucus and dead cells on the inflamed colon.
glossary.Gram-positive: Bacteria with a thick cell wall that stains purple with Gram stain.
glossary.spores: Tough dormant bacterial forms that survive heat, drying and alcohol.
glossary.GDH: Glutamate dehydrogenase: a C. difficile antigen showing the organism is present, not that it is producing toxin.
glossary.colonisation: Carrying an organism without it causing disease.
glossary.toxin A: C. difficile enterotoxin that damages the colonic lining.
glossary.toxin B: C. difficile cytotoxin, the main cause of colonic cell damage.
glossary.toxic megacolon: Acute, non-obstructive dilatation of the colon with systemic toxicity; risks perforation.
glossary.ileus: Loss of normal gut movement, with distension and absent bowel sounds.
glossary.transmural: Through the full thickness of the bowel wall.
glossary.PPI: Proton pump inhibitor, such as omeprazole, which reduces stomach acid.
glossary.omeprazole: A proton pump inhibitor; a risk factor for C. difficile.
glossary.broad-spectrum antibiotics: Antibiotics that kill a wide range of bacteria, including normal gut flora.
glossary.clindamycin: A broad-spectrum antibiotic strongly associated with C. difficile.
glossary.cephalosporins: Beta-lactam antibiotics such as ceftriaxone; a major C. difficile risk.
glossary.co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid; a broad-spectrum penicillin linked to C. difficile.
glossary.vancomycin: Glycopeptide antibiotic; given orally it stays in the gut to treat C. difficile.
glossary.fidaxomicin: A narrow-spectrum oral antibiotic for C. difficile, used second-line or for recurrence.
glossary.metronidazole: An antibiotic for anaerobes; given IV with oral vancomycin in life-threatening C. difficile.
glossary.clarithromycin: A macrolide antibiotic used for severe Campylobacter infection.
glossary.loperamide: An antimotility drug; avoided in C. difficile because it can cause toxic megacolon.
glossary.antimicrobial stewardship: Using antibiotics only when needed, at the right dose and for the right time.
glossary.colonic flora: The normal bacteria of the colon that keep pathogens like C. difficile in check.
glossary.Campylobacter: Commonest UK bacterial cause of bloody diarrhoea, often from undercooked chicken.
glossary.Shigella: A Gram-negative bacillus causing bloody dysentery; very few organisms are infective.
glossary.Salmonella: A Gram-negative bacterium spread by eggs and poultry, causing diarrhoea and fever.
glossary.E. coli O157: A toxin-producing E. coli causing bloody diarrhoea and haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
glossary.HUS: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome: haemolysis, low platelets and kidney injury after E. coli O157.
glossary.Entamoeba histolytica: A parasite causing amoebic dysentery and liver abscess, acquired through travel.
glossary.oral rehydration solution: A salt and sugar drink that replaces fluid and electrolytes lost in diarrhoea.
glossary.ORS: Oral rehydration solution: the first-line fluid replacement in diarrhoea.
glossary.WCC: White cell count; above 15 ×10⁹/L marks severe C. difficile.
glossary.AKI: Acute kidney injury: a rapid rise in creatinine or fall in urine output.
glossary.side room: A single isolation room, ideally with its own toilet, to stop spread on the ward.

technique.stem: An 84 year old care home resident was treated with ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection 10 days ago. She takes lansoprazole. She now has 2 days of profuse watery, foul-smelling diarrhoea with crampy lower abdominal pain. There is no blood. Her abdomen is diffusely tender but not distended.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about diarrhoea in an older patient.
Recent antibiotic, PPI, care home, watery foul stools, diffuse tenderness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Usually bloody diarrhoea with fever after undercooked chicken.
Sudden left-sided pain with bloody diarrhoea in vascular patients.
Constipation history and a loaded rectum, not after antibiotics.
A first presentation at 84 is uncommon and usually bloody.

steps.x: **B. C. difficile colitis.** Rule: antibiotics + PPI + new watery diarrhoea = C. difficile.

technique.stem: A 72 year old man on a surgical ward develops 6 episodes of watery diarrhoea 4 days after starting co-amoxiclav. A stool sample is sent. The ward wants to know whether he needs treatment.
technique.q: Which result confirms active C. difficile infection?

steps.x: The question is infection versus carriage.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Shows colonisation or exposure only.
Shows inflammation, not the cause.
Non-specific.
Normal flora is expected and does not confirm C. difficile.

steps.x: **B. Toxin positive.** Rule: antigen = there; toxin = disease.

technique.stem: A 79 year old woman has confirmed C. difficile infection and has started oral vancomycin. She is in a side room. A student nurse asks how to clean her hands after helping the patient to the commode.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate hand hygiene?
o: No hand hygiene needed if gloves were worn

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Soap and water hand washing, plus gloves and aprons.

elim: Does not kill C. difficile spores.
Still does not remove spores.
Not the standard; washing is required.
Hands are washed after removing gloves.

steps.x: **E. Soap and water.** Rule: gel does not kill spores.

technique.stem: On an elderly care ward, three patients develop C. difficile infection in a week. All staff use alcohol hand gel between patients. An infection control nurse recommends switching to soap and water.
technique.q: Which best explains why alcohol gel failed to prevent spread?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Spores are not killed by alcohol; washing removes them.

elim: Unrelated to hand hygiene.
It is a bacterium.
It is Gram-positive, and Gram stain does not decide alcohol resistance.
Spread is faecal-oral via spores.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man was given IV ceftriaxone for pneumonia 8 days ago and takes omeprazole. He now has profuse green, foul-smelling watery diarrhoea and abdominal cramps. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Profuse green, foul watery diarrhoea after a cephalosporin in a patient on a PPI is C. difficile. Campylobacter and Salmonella are community acquired with bloody stools.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Bloody diarrhoea after undercooked chicken, in the community.
Needs travel and causes bloody diarrhoea.
Vomiting-predominant, short-lived, outbreaks; not linked to antibiotics.
Food-borne, community acquired, with bloody stools or fever.

steps.x: **B. C. difficile.** Antibiotics + PPI + watery green stools.

practice.stem: A 23 year old man has 3 days of bloody diarrhoea, crampy abdominal pain and fever. Two days before it started he ate chicken from a barbecue that was pink in the middle. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg and respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Bloody diarrhoea with fever a few days after undercooked chicken is Campylobacter colitis, usually self-limiting. B. cereus and S. aureus cause vomiting within hours.

steps.x: An organism question with a food history.

clues: chicken from a barbecue that was pink
steps.x: Undercooked poultry, 2 to 5 day incubation, bloody diarrhoea, fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Vomiting within hours of reheated rice.
No antibiotic or hospital exposure, and usually not bloody.
Needs travel and is gradual.
Vomiting within hours from preformed toxin.

steps.x: **B. Campylobacter.** Usually self-limiting; clarithromycin only if severe.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman returned from 6 weeks volunteering in rural India a month ago. Over 3 weeks she has developed increasingly frequent loose stools containing blood and mucus, with lower abdominal discomfort. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Gradual bloody diarrhoea with mucus after travel to an endemic area, with red-cell-containing trophozoites, is amoebic colitis (Entamoeba histolytica). Giardia is non-bloody.

steps.x: Travel, gradual onset, bloody mucus stools.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No antibiotic or hospital exposure.
Non-bloody, greasy diarrhoea with bloating.
Acute vomiting and watery diarrhoea over 1 to 3 days.
Profuse rice-water diarrhoea, not bloody.

steps.x: **B. Entamoeba histolytica.** Bloody diarrhoea + travel = parasitic.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman on an orthopaedic ward has 2 loose stools a day after starting flucloxacillin. She is well and her abdomen is soft and non-tender. A stool sample is tested.
practice.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of these results?
practice.e: A positive C. difficile antigen with a negative toxin indicates colonisation or exposure, not active infection; toxin positivity is needed for true infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: She is well, with no toxin.
Infection requires toxin positivity.
No toxin and a normal WCC.
Her abdomen is soft and she is well.

steps.x: **A. Colonisation.** Rule: antigen alone does not mean disease.

practice.stem: An 80 year old man has toxin-positive C. difficile diarrhoea, 8 times a day. His abdomen is tender but not distended and bowel sounds are present. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most accurate assessment of severity?
practice.e: A WCC over 15 or a creatinine rise over 50% from baseline defines severe C. difficile infection. Life-threatening disease needs shock, ileus, CT dilatation or toxic megacolon.

steps.x: WCC 18.4 (>15) and creatinine 92 → 151 (66% rise), but no shock or megacolon.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: He is toxin positive with diarrhoea.
He is not shocked and has no ileus or dilatation.
His WCC and creatinine rise exceed the cut-offs.
WCC above 15 makes it severe.

steps.x: **E. Severe.** Rule: WCC >15 or creatinine up >50% = severe.

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman with C. difficile infection had been passing 10 stools a day, but over 12 hours the diarrhoea has stopped. Her abdomen is distended and tender with absent bowel sounds. She was given codeine for pain. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 86/52 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Abdominal X-ray shows a transverse colon diameter of 8 cm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sudden cessation of diarrhoea with distension, absent bowel sounds, shock and a colon over 6 cm in C. difficile is toxic megacolon; opioids predispose to it.

clues: distended and tender with absent bowel sounds
steps.x: Diarrhoea stops (not improvement), distension, shock, colon >6 cm, opioid given.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No previous surgery is mentioned, and the dilated bowel is colon.
Stopping diarrhoea with distension and shock is deterioration, not recovery.
Gives a coffee-bean sigmoid, not dilated transverse colon in colitis.
Not toxic and febrile with shock.

steps.x: **D. Toxic megacolon.** Rule: 'diarrhoea stopped' + distension in C. difficile = megacolon.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has 4 days of bloody diarrhoea and fever after eating at a street food market. She has had no antibiotics. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the cause?
practice.e: Stool culture (with PCR) identifies the bacterial cause of community-acquired bloody diarrhoea. Calprotectin shows inflammation but not the organism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Shows dilatation, not the organism.
May help in sepsis but rarely identify colitis pathogens.
Not first-line for acute infective diarrhoea.
Shows inflammation, not the organism.

steps.x: **E. Stool culture.** Rule: stool culture and toxin testing are the gold standard.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man with severe C. difficile infection develops increasing abdominal distension and pain. He is still passing loose stool. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 102/64 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to assess severity?
practice.e: CT abdomen is used when severe C. difficile is suspected, to look for dilatation, ileus or perforation. Barium and colonoscopy risk perforation.

steps.x: Suspected complication: dilatation, ileus or perforation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Contraindicated in severe colitis: perforation risk.
Perforation risk in severe colitis.
Already confirmed; does not assess severity.
Gas-filled bowel limits it.

steps.x: **C. CT abdomen.** Rule: severe disease suspected → CT.

practice.stem: A 67 year old woman has a first episode of toxin-positive C. difficile infection after co-amoxiclav. Her abdomen is soft. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Oral vancomycin for 10 days is first-line, with the causative antibiotic stopped. Fidaxomicin is second-line; IV metronidazole is added only if life-threatening.

steps.x: Initial management of a first episode.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral vancomycin for 10 days; stop the co-amoxiclav; isolate.

elim: Does not reach the colon lumen.
Antimotility drugs risk toxic megacolon.
Stopping the culprit is right, but toxin-positive diarrhoea also needs oral vancomycin.
Reserved for life-threatening disease.

steps.x: **D. Oral vancomycin.** Rule: first episode = oral vancomycin 10 days.

practice.stem: A 73 year old man completed 10 days of oral vancomycin for C. difficile infection 5 weeks ago, and his diarrhoea settled. He now has watery diarrhoea again and his stool is toxin positive. He is haemodynamically stable with a soft abdomen.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Recurrence within 12 weeks of resolution, or failure to respond, is treated with oral fidaxomicin second-line.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Not effective alone and not the recurrence treatment.
Contraindicated in C. difficile.
A cause of C. difficile, not a treatment.
For recurrence within 12 weeks, fidaxomicin is preferred.

steps.x: **D. Fidaxomicin.** Rule: recurrence within 12 weeks = fidaxomicin.

practice.stem: An 82 year old woman with C. difficile infection becomes confused. Her abdomen is distended. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. CT shows a dilated colon with partial ileus.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antimicrobial treatment?
practice.e: Life-threatening C. difficile (shock, ileus, dilatation) is treated with oral vancomycin and IV metronidazole together, with urgent surgical review.

steps.x: Shock and ileus on CT: life-threatening.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral vancomycin AND IV metronidazole, plus surgical review.

elim: Oral vancomycin is still needed for the colonic lumen.
Does not reach the colon.
Second-line, not for life-threatening disease.
Not enough for life-threatening disease.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: life-threatening = oral vancomycin + IV metronidazole.

practice.stem: A 77 year old man has C. difficile infection after a course of clindamycin. Flexible sigmoidoscopy shows multiple raised yellow plaques on an inflamed colonic mucosa.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the mucosal damage?
o: Colonocyte damage by toxins A and B
Direct bacterial invasion of the bowel wall
practice.e: C. difficile produces toxins A and B, which damage colonic mucosal cells and cause the raised yellow pseudomembranes. It does not invade the bowel wall.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Toxins A and B damage colonic mucosal cells, forming pseudomembranes.

elim: C. difficile is non-invasive; damage is toxin-mediated.
Not the mechanism of C. difficile colitis.
Causes ischaemic colitis, not pseudomembranes after antibiotics.
That is S. aureus or B. cereus food poisoning.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: C. difficile damage is toxin-mediated.
